title: Facing the House
hook: wherever you are, you face the Ka'ba in Mecca

segments.voice: Yesterday: taharah, cleanness of body, clothes and place. Your line was a clean corner. Did you leave one small spot clearer than you found it? Day ninety-nine.

Open almost any hotel room in Istanbul, Kuala Lumpur or Dubai, and somewhere, on the ceiling, in a drawer, or on a little sticker by the desk, there's an arrow. It isn't pointing to the exit. Open a prayer app in Chicago, and a compass needle swings and settles. Walk into a mosque anywhere, and there's a niche in one wall, the mihrab, and every line of people stands facing it. Two billion possible starting points, and all of them are turning toward one small building in one valley. Today: the direction everyone faces.
screen: `AN ARROW IN A HOTEL ROOM.` → `A NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `ALL FACING ONE BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The word is qiblah, the direction a person faces in prayer. It comes from a root that means to face, to be in front of. The qiblah is the Ka'ba, the cube-shaped House in Mecca that the Qur'an says Ibrahim and Isma'il raised. But it wasn't always. For the first years, including the early months in Medina, the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem. Then, the Qur'an says in Surah al-Baqarah, the Prophet ﷺ kept turning his face toward the sky, and the verse came: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. The hadith collections tell what happened next. A man who had prayed with the Prophet passed a mosque where people were in the middle of their prayer, still facing Jerusalem, and told them. And they turned around, mid-prayer, to face Mecca. There's a mosque in Medina still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. Here's the idea underneath. The same passage says that the East and the West belong to Allah, and wherever you turn, there is His face. So Muslims don't say God lives in the Ka'ba. The direction isn't about where God is. It's about where the people are pointed: one direction, so a worshipper in Jakarta and one in Lagos are part of the same line. And here's an honest wrinkle. On a round earth, the shortest path from North America to Mecca runs northeast, over the top of the globe. Most North American Muslims face northeast. Some older communities face southeast, following a flat map. Both are trying to face the same House.
screen: `QIBLAH — THE DIRECTION YOU FACE.` · `FIRST JERUSALEM, THEN MECCA.` · `THEY TURNED IN THE MIDDLE OF PRAYER.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, HIS FACE.` · then, large: `ONE DIRECTION, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the qiblah from where you are. If you have a compass or a phone app, use it. If not, just work it out roughly: Mecca is in western Arabia, so from most of North America it's northeast, from Europe southeast, from India roughly west. Turn your body that way. Stand or sit still for a moment. Picture the lines of people all over the earth, all facing the same point you are. If you pray, this is where you'd face. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah. The direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba in Mecca, turned from Jerusalem in the Prophet's time. Today's word.
Your line: all turned one way. Once today, when you notice which way you're facing, remember the people, somewhere, facing the same point. Day ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for every prayer; mosques mark the direction with a niche called the mihrab, and many people use a compass or a phone app when they pray away from home.

stop and start the prayer over

original.note: Arabic: the direction faced in prayer, from a root meaning to face, to be in front of.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims face Mecca.
what it means: the qiblah is the Ka'ba, and facing it puts every worshipper on earth in the same line.
what a scholar hears: the change from Jerusalem to Mecca in Medina (2:142–150), and the debate over great-circle versus flat-map directions in North America.

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. Bukhari 40 has a man passing a mosque in Medina; Bukhari 403 has the people of Quba at the dawn prayer. The script tells it generally and names the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs; a Keeper may want the exact attribution (Banu Salimah) of that mosque.
Whether Muslims faced Jerusalem throughout the Meccan period is discussed by scholars; the script says 'for the first years, including the early months in Medina'.
North American qiblah (northeast great circle vs. southeast rhumb line): the northeast view is the majority, stated as 'most'; please confirm the framing.
Rough directions in the practice (NE from North America, SE from Europe, a little north of west from India) are approximate; please check.
